paragraphs.heading: The three laws
paragraphs.text: Newton gave three laws of motion. The first says a body stays still, or keeps moving at a steady speed in a straight line, unless a force acts on it. The second says that at any moment the net force on a body equals its mass times its acceleration, which is the same as how fast its momentum is changing. The third says that when two bodies push or pull on each other, the two forces are equal in size and point in opposite directions.

paragraphs.heading: Where they came from
paragraphs.text: Isaac Newton first set out the laws in his Philosophiæ Naturalis Principia Mathematica, published in 1687. He used them to explain how many kinds of objects and systems move. Later thinkers, drawing especially on the idea of energy, built classical mechanics on top of his work. In modern times the laws were found to have limits, and quantum mechanics and relativity were developed for more extreme cases.

paragraphs.heading: Treating bodies as points
paragraphs.text: The laws are often stated for point masses, bodies whose size can be ignored. That works for real objects when their inner parts' motion does not matter and when they are far apart compared with their own size. The Earth and the Sun can both be treated as points when working out the Earth's orbit. But the Earth is not a point when you study what happens on its surface.

paragraphs.heading: Describing motion with numbers
paragraphs.text: Kinematics, the maths of describing motion, gives positions as numbers that change over time. Picture a bead sliding on a track running left to right: its place is its distance from a chosen zero point, negative on the left and positive on the right. If its position over time is s(t), its average velocity between t₀ and t₁ is the change in position divided by the change in time, Δs/Δt, where the Greek letter Δ means change in. Calculus sharpens this into instantaneous velocity, the speed and direction at a single moment, written v = ds/dt.

paragraphs.heading: Vectors and forces
paragraphs.text: Position, velocity and acceleration are vectors: quantities with both a size and a direction. A velocity of 𝐯 = (3 m/s, 4 m/s), for example, means moving 3 metres per second along the horizontal and 4 metres per second along the vertical. In physics, force puts a number on the everyday idea of a push or a pull, and it is a vector too. In Newton's mechanics, forces often come from strings and ropes, friction, muscles and gravity.

paragraphs.heading: Inertia
paragraphs.text: Physics gives some everyday words special meanings: force is not the same as power or pressure, and mass is not the same as weight. Newton's first law states the principle of inertia, which says a body's natural behaviour is to travel in a straight line at a steady speed. Left alone, a body keeps doing what it was doing, but outside forces can disturb that.

paragraphs.heading: Who is really moving
paragraphs.text: Today the first law is read as saying that no inertial observer is special. Someone standing on the ground watching a train pass is an inertial observer. If the train runs smoothly in a straight line at a steady speed, a passenger sitting on board is one too, and feels no motion. There is no way to say which of them is truly moving and which is truly still. What looks like rest to one looks like steady straight-line motion to the other, and no experiment can pick a winner.
